intro: Chief executives have some of the strongest leadership skills of any career, so their matches pay less. The closest of the 25 careers below is Treasurers and Controllers, with an 81% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $166,570 for its broader group, below the $213,990 chief executives earn.
why_it_works: Leading an organization means setting direction, managing money and people at scale, and owning the hardest decisions. O*NET rates judgment and decision making at 4.75 out of 5 for this job, among the highest scores for any career. Finance, sales and public relations leadership use the same skills on a narrower scope. None of the 25 matches pays more. All need no extra education.
tips: Board, advisory and interim roles keep your experience in use but are not separate careers in this data.
Financial Managers are a 79% match if you want to focus on money rather than the whole organization.
Teaching or mentoring is a common next step; instructing is one of your main skill gaps.

faq.q: What jobs can former chief executives do?
faq.a: The closest matches are treasurers and controllers (81%), Financial Managers (79%) and Public Relations Managers (73%), based on O*NET 31.0. Sales Managers are 72% matched and earn $148,270, which is 31% less than the $213,990 chief executive median, but with a narrower scope.

faq.q: Do any careers for chief executives pay more?
faq.a: None of the 25 matches pays more. The highest are Industrial-Organizational Psychologists at $193,950 (9% less), Computer and Information Systems Managers at $175,140 (18% less) and architectural and engineering managers at $171,270 (20% less), according to BLS May 2025 data.

faq.q: Do chief executives need more education to switch?
faq.a: No. All 25 matches need no more education than chief executives already have, including all of the top 10. A bachelor's degree is common in close matches, held by 56% of workers in one of them, so leadership experience is what counts.

faq.q: What skills would chief executives need for a new role?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are service orientation, instructing, programming and operations analysis. Complex problem solving already rates 4.38 out of 5 for chief executives in O*NET, so teaching or hands-on technical work is the main change for most people.
